analysis.one_liner: Bans price gouging on rent and home sales during declared housing emergencies and investigates institutional investors.
analysis.headline: The HOME Act of 2023 was referred to two House committees on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it unlawful to charge unconscionably excessive rents or home prices in areas where the President declares a housing emergency, with penalties enforced by HUD and state attorneys general. It would also create a unit inside HUD to monitor housing markets and corporate landlord activity, trigger investigations when large investors buy too many homes in one area, and require the regulator of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac to attach renter protections to mortgages on multifamily housing. Penalties would go into a trust fund that builds affordable rental housing.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters and homebuyers, especially in areas hit by a declared housing emergency or heavy institutional-investor buying. Tenants in buildings whose mortgages are bought by Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac would gain protections against steep rent increases. Extremely low- and very low-income families benefit from the penalty-funded affordable housing trust fund.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Renters and homebuyers facing gouging and large landlords

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful to rent or sell housing at unconscionably excessive prices during a President-declared housing emergency, with HUD and state attorneys general empowered to seek injunctions, civil penalties, and restitution for residents [S2][S3].
Creates a Housing Monitoring and Enforcement Unit at HUD to track rental and single-family market data and identify market manipulation [S2][S3].

Requires HUD to investigate when a single buyer purchases more than 5% of single-family homes sold in a market area over three years, or large institutional investors collectively buy more than 25% in one year [S2][S3].

Directs the Federal Housing Finance Agency to set standards for Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac purchases of multifamily mortgages so that tenants get basic protections and are shielded from egregious rent increases [S2][S3].
Deposits collected penalties into the Housing Trust Fund to expand and preserve rental housing affordable to extremely low- and very low-income families, including homeless families [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large landlords, corporate owners of single-family rentals, and institutional investors who would face price-gouging enforcement, investigations of their purchasing, and antitrust reviews of information sharing. Lenders selling multifamily mortgages to Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac would face renter-protection conditions.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large corporate landlords and institutional home investors

drawbacks.text: Emergency price limits can suppress supply when it is needed most; the bill acknowledges this by letting sellers escape liability if a price increase reflects higher costs or added risk, and by rewarding landlords who add units during an emergency, but critics of price-gouging caps generally argue they discourage the new supply and investment that housing shortages require [S3].

The bill leans heavily on studies, monitoring, and reports — a $1 million HUD investigation, a new data unit, an FTC-Justice Department antitrust review, and annual reports — rather than directly increasing housing supply, and the price-gouging ban applies only during declared emergencies lasting up to 30 days at a time [S3].

The vague standard of 'unconscionably excessive' pricing, enforced through FTC-style enforcement powers, could create unpredictable legal exposure for ordinary small landlords as well as large ones [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For renters in overheated markets and areas struck by disasters, the emergency gouging ban and the multifamily renter protections offer real, if conditional, help, and the penalty-funded affordable housing trust fund is a concrete gain. The bill's biggest limitation is that most of its content is oversight and study rather than building more housing, so it attacks abusive pricing and concentrated ownership without addressing the supply shortage that pushes prices up in the first place.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Financial Services and Judiciary committees the day it was introduced, and neither committee ever held a hearing or vote, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Steven Horsford (D-NV) introduced the bill on February 1, 2023 [S1][S5].
The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and, in addition, to the House Judiciary Committee for consideration of provisions within their jurisdiction [S5].
No further action was ever recorded: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote in the House, and the bill never received a Senate vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S1][S5].
Ten House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican did [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large landlords, institutional homebuyers, and the broader real estate industry are better off because the bill never advanced: it faced no price-gouging enforcement, no scrutiny of bulk home purchases, no antitrust review of information sharing, and no renter protections attached to Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac multifamily mortgages.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Corporate landlords and institutional home investors

for.name: Rep. Steven Horsford
for.what_they_did: Introduced the HOME Act of 2023 and referred it to the Financial Services and Judiciary Committees.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of primary referral, chaired by Rep. Patrick McHenry
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill after receiving the referral in February 2023.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Never took action on the provisions referred to it for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so no voting split exists in the record; all sponsorship and cosponsorship came from Democrats, and the committees that buried the bill were chaired by Republicans.

industries.industry: Large landlords and institutional investors in single-family rentals
industries.note: The bill would expose them to price-gouging enforcement during declared emergencies, HUD investigations when they buy more than 5% of homes in a market area (or 25% collectively in a year), and antitrust review of information sharing. Their business model of bulk-purchasing housing and pricing rents against limited competition is what the bill targets.

industries.industry: Real estate industry broadly (developers, managers, brokers)
industries.note: HUD would be required to consider the impact of mergers and acquisitions in the industry, and the Justice Department and FTC would review anti-competitive behaviors including information sharing. This is oversight and enforcement risk rather than a direct restriction on building or selling housing.

industries.industry: Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac multifamily mortgage market
industries.note: The bill requires the enterprises' regulator to attach basic renter protections and limits on egregious rent increases to multifamily mortgages they buy. Lenders and landlords who rely on this financing would face new conditions, while tenants in financed buildings gain protections.
